Any bytes can be cached, but a CDN does not cache 'whatever it gets' automatically. Cloudflare 'does not cache HTML or JSON by default' (it caches by file extension) and skips responses with Cache-Control private/no-store/no-cache, max-age=0 or Set-Cookie; JSON/API caching needs explicit cache rules or headers.
precise_version: A CDN can cache any bytes - images, JSON, HTML - but only responses it is told are cacheable (by origin Cache-Control headers or CDN cache rules); many CDNs do not cache HTML/JSON by default.

S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability and 99.99% availability over a year - not 'nine nines'. Durability (not losing data) and availability are different guarantees from a CDN's latency benefit.
precise_version: S3 is designed for eleven nines of durability and 99.99% availability; a CDN instead gives lower latency by serving from nearby edges.

Mixes three separate things. A signed URL's validity comes from the expiration date/time written into its signed policy - not from the cache TTL (how long the edge keeps the object) and not from a certificate's lifetime (the signing key pair is long-lived). CloudFront compares the expiration time in the URL with the current time on each request.
precise_version: The URL is short-lived because the backend signs it with a short expiry time; after that the CDN rejects it, regardless of how long the photo stays cached.

Over-generalised. Strict privacy is a trade-off, not 'no CDN': you can keep the CDN and shrink the exposure with very short-lived signed URLs or signed cookies, custom policies restricted to the viewer's IP range, or edge token checks; content can also be encrypted client-side so cached bytes are useless without the key. Routing every byte through API servers is one option, not the only one.
precise_version: Stronger privacy means tighter controls - very short-lived, IP-bound signed URLs/cookies, edge auth, or encrypting the media - or, at the extreme, serving every byte through your own authorised servers.

Conflates two techniques. DNS-based mapping (Akamai): the hostname CNAMEs to an edge hostname and the CDN's own authoritative DNS returns the IP of a good nearby server - the resolver just asks. Anycast (Cloudflare): every location announces the same IP via BGP and 'the network itself will direct traffic to the nearest' data center - no per-user DNS answer needed. BGP is not what the DNS resolver uses.
precise_version: CDNs steer users to a nearby edge either with their own DNS answering per location (Akamai-style mapping) or with anycast, where one IP is announced from every PoP via BGP and internet routing picks the nearest.

note: Exact tuning is proprietary, but the mechanisms are public: Cloudflare documents anycast, Akamai documents its DNS edge-hostname mapping (and has published research on end-user mapping).
